title: One fine night
hook: don't chase the past, don't pin hopes on the future; see what is here, today

segments.voice: Yesterday: Yama's questions, and your line, the messengers came. Did a baby or an elder carry a message to you? Today, a short verse that answers it. Day four hundred ninety-nine.

Scroll back through old photos for ten minutes and see how you feel. Then open a calendar and plan next year for ten minutes. Two very different moods, and in both of them you've left the room you're sitting in. The hundred and thirty-first discourse is short, and at its heart is a verse of just a few lines. The Buddha recites it at Jeta's Grove near Savatthi, then explains it. It's one of the very few verses in the Middle-Length Sayings that gets four whole discourses of its own. Today: bhaddekaratta.
screen: `TEN MINUTES IN OLD PHOTOS.` → `TEN MINUTES IN NEXT YEAR.` → `A VERSE WITH FOUR DISCOURSES.`

segments.voice: Here's what the verse says, in paraphrase. Don't chase after the past. Don't build your hopes on the future. The past is already left behind. The future hasn't come. Whatever is present, see it clearly, right where it is, steady and unshaken. Do today what needs doing with energy. Who knows, death may come tomorrow, and there's no bargaining with death and his great army. Whoever lives this way, keen, day and night, the peaceful sage calls one who has had a bhaddekaratta. And what is that word? Bhadda means good, fortunate, auspicious. Eka means one. Ratta is the hard part. It can mean night, so one good night, or one auspicious day and night. Some translators read it differently and render the whole word as something like one fine attachment, or a single excellent night. Scholars honestly disagree, and the commentary's reading isn't the only one. What's clear is the shape of the teaching. Then the Buddha explains how people chase the past: thinking, I had such a body, such feelings, such thoughts, and finding delight there. How they build hopes on the future: I'll have such a body, such feelings. And how, in the present, they take body or feeling or mind as a self, and get pulled along. The one who doesn't is the one having that fine night. Not a night of special visions. A night, or a day, lived where it actually is. After yesterday's messengers, this is the answer: not fear, but full attention to the only day there is.
screen: `DON'T CHASE THE PAST` · `DON'T PIN HOPES ON THE FUTURE` · `SEE WHAT IS HERE, TODAY` · `BHADDA, EKA, RATTA` · then, large: `ONE FINE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: live one day this way. Start now, for two minutes. Sit, and each time the mind slides into a memory, say softly: past. Each time it jumps to a plan, say: future. Then come back to what's actually here: this breath, this sound, this weight. You don't have to hate the past or the future. You're just choosing, for now, the room you're in. The bell holds the time.
Bhaddekaratta. One fine night, an auspicious day: not chasing the past, not hoping on the future, seeing what's here clearly, today. Today's word.
Your line: one fine night. Today, catch yourself once in old photos and once in next year, and come back to the room you're actually in. Day four hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: The Bhaddekaratta verse is chanted in some Theravada monasteries and is a favorite of meditation teachers in several traditions, who often use it to teach dwelling in the present moment.

fork.setup: you've caught yourself delighting in how things used to be. what does the Buddha's explanation call that?
fork.reveal: thinking 'I had such a body, such feelings' and finding delight there is reviving the past, in the Buddha's explanation.

original.note: Pali bhaddekaratta: bhadda, good; eka, one; ratta, perhaps night. its exact sense is debated.

trapdoor: what you thought: one fine night means a lovely evening out.
what it means: a day and night lived fully in the present, not chasing the past or the future.
what a scholar hears: bhaddekaratta's last element is disputed (ratta as night or as attached), and MN 131–134 are four discourses built on the same verse.
